title: Choosing the Right Model
description: Train three different surrogates on the same 3-input nonlinear dataset and compare their cross-validation scores. You will see why model choice matters and when GPR outperforms Random Forest and Linear models.

steps.instruction: The dataset has 3 inputs (x1, x2, x3) and 1 output (y). Notice the input ranges: x1 and x2 span roughly −π to +π, x3 spans 0 to 5.

Open the scatter matrix. The x1 vs y and x2 vs y plots will look noisy — that is because all three inputs affect y at once, hiding each individual trend. Look carefully at x1 vs y for a faint curved, wave-like pattern. The x3 vs y plot should show a clearer upward trend. You will compare three models on this data: Linear (assumes straight-line relationships only), Random Forest (builds many decision trees, handles curves and interactions), and GPR — Gaussian Process Regression (learns correlation between nearby data points, works well on smooth responses with limited data).

quiz.question: Given that x1 and x2 have a curved, wave-like relationship with y, which model type would you expect to struggle most?
quiz.explanation: A linear model can only draw a straight line through the data. It has no way to capture a wave-shaped pattern without manually adding transformed features. GPR and Random Forest can both fit curved responses directly, which is why they will outperform Linear on this dataset.

steps.instruction: Designate x1, x2, x3 as inputs and y as the output.
Apply Min-Max normalization to all three inputs.

First run: configure as Linear model, test split 0.2, 5-fold CV. Train and note the R² score. The Results panel will show two R² values — Test Set Performance and CV (cross-validation). They measure slightly different things.

quiz.question: The Results panel shows both Test Set R² and CV R². What does CV R² measure that makes it more reliable than simply measuring accuracy on the training data?
options: Accuracy on the 20% held-out test rows
Average accuracy across 5 rounds where a different portion of the training data is held out each time — the model never trains on those rows
Accuracy on all rows including training
quiz.explanation: CV R² splits the training data into 5 groups. Each time, it trains on 4 groups and tests on the 5th — repeating until every group has been the test set once. The average score is more reliable than a single split because it tests the model on more varied data. A model that simply memorises the training data would score high on training accuracy but low on CV.

steps.instruction: Note the test R² for Linear. Now go back to Step 8 — Model, switch to GPR, and retrain. Then try Random Forest. Which model achieves the highest test R²?

quiz.question: For this 150-row, 3-input, smooth nonlinear dataset, what is the most likely ranking of models by test R²?
quiz.explanation: GPR wins on smooth, small datasets where its correlation-based kernel fits the underlying pattern precisely. Random Forest is more general and handles noise well but is less efficient on smooth low-dimensional data. Linear cannot represent the curved response at all, so it scores lowest. Both GPR and RF far outperform Linear here.

steps.instruction: Use the best-performing model to predict y at x1=0, x2=0, x3=2.5. The true value is sin(0)·cos(0) + 0.3×2.5 = 0.75.
